entries.text: Doom Has an Address · v7 · Canon Chapter 07 · Later in Arc 1 Mikhail's mock blessing becomes a prolonged argument over ancestry, porcelain, and Lynleit's private life. Once she looks away, he lets one silence pass without a joke. Lynleit and Kyrien destroy a Holumn together and complete the final condition of its mechanism. The Holumn transfers one terminal curse across both identities, causing progressive physical decline and a prognosis measured first in weeks and then in days. Suppressing the curse in either person fails because the remaining attachment reconstructs it in the other. The traditional solution requires one of them to die first so the surviving identity is released. Lynleit rejects the fatal solution, consults other Magi, and searches Magiarchal records and prohibited theurgical procedures for an alternative. Natalia uses a two-name diagram, her failed decision diary, and her experience after leaving the Academy to explain why a change of identity must go deeper than its description. She introduces the ego hypothesis and quotes Jung. Lynleit jokes with Natalia, works through the examples, and keeps the diagram; Natalia proposes reciprocal attachment as a possible change, not a guaranteed cure. Father Mikhail reaches the same conclusion through Church records and tells Lynleit that physical intimacy could work only if an existing attachment changes both identities. Mikhail names Inanna and describes Lynleit's lineage as preserving a three-thousand-year association with the Cult; she objects to using that history as a personal obligation. Lynleit's handling of her cup, increasingly formal objections, and threatened reprisal suggest how personally Mikhail's mock praise has struck her. inferred Mikhail leaving Lynleit's averted gaze unremarked suggests that he recognizes when his teasing has reached something she cannot easily answer. inferred Lynleit withholds the proposed method from Kyrien and investigates their relationship as a possible procedure. Lynleit attempts to initiate an encounter but does not fully cross the boundary between them. The curse begins weakening the following morning and is later gone. Lynleit's unread pages and repeated denials suggest that she still wants Kyrien now that the curse is gone. inferred Kyrien suspects a connection between Lynleit’s attempt and their recovery, but she withholds the proposed treatment. The incomplete attempt and its aftermath change both identities enough for the curse to lose its hold. Doom Has an Address The condition The Holumn was eventually destroyed. That was the first mistake. Lynleit and Kyrien did not understand what they were fighting until after they had already killed it. Destroying the creature completed the final part of its mechanism: its own terminal condition passed to whoever had caused its death. They had destroyed it together. There was still only one curse, attached to both of them. Their bodies began to weaken. Sleep stopped restoring them properly, and minor injuries healed too slowly. Lynleit found her magecraft increasingly exhausting. Kyrien began stopping on stairs. Within days, ordinary exertion had become difficult for both of them. The Magi who examined the curse gave them several weeks. Attempts to suppress it produced a second discovery. Removing it from Lynleit brought relief only until the attachment to Kyrien restored it. Treating him produced the same result in reverse. One of them could survive if the other died first. Lynleit rejected the answer. She spoke to other Magi, searched Magiarchal records, and investigated prohibited theurgical procedures. Could memory erasure work? A coma? Destroying magical capacity? Every answer sent her back to the same choice. Having one of them declared dead would not help either. The curse had no interest in legal language. Eventually she called Natalia. The academically respectable answer Natalia was silent long enough that Lynleit checked the connection. "Natalia?" "I'm here. Find something to write on." Lynleit pulled a sheet out from under a report. "Should I put my name at the top?" "Twice, if it helps." "It rarely helped with your marking." "Two names, then. Yours and Kyrien's." Lynleit wrote them side by side. "Join them," Natalia said. "Now cross yours out." The pen stopped. "On the paper, Lynleit." "I know. I was enjoying the lesson." "If I gave that sheet to someone who knew Kyrien, could they still find you?" "Through him." "And if you crossed out his name instead?" "They could ask me." "There. Suppression rubs out part of the address. It leaves someone who can supply the missing part." Lynleit looked at the line between the names. She had drawn it through an old calculation. "So they keep treating us as separate patients." "Which is a sensible place to begin. Unfortunately, you have already tested it." "Several times." "And nearly exhausted yourselves proving the same thing. Keep that sheet. We're going to stop repeating it." Lynleit drew a small, unfriendly face beside her name. "This is older than your Holumn," Natalia continued. "The mechanism, I mean. People have been trying to move a death from one person to another for a very long time." "With results?" "The Assyrians had a substitute-king ritual. A fatal omen threatened the king, so another man occupied his place and received his fate." "Comforting." "The useful question is why the omen would accept the substitute. It wasn't looking for the king's face. It recognized a position someone else could occupy." "And ours recognizes the people who killed it." "Yes. Usually you hear stories about a creature hiding its life in an egg, or an animal, or a locked box. Killing the body doesn't finish the job." Lynleit turned the pen over. "This one hid its death in us." "Exactly." She stopped drawing. "Then the usual solution really is what they told me." "One dies first." The words settled badly between them. Lynleit stared out the window. "I'm not doing that." "I assumed as much." "There has to be another way." "There usually is. People just become lazy when death works reliably." Lynleit closed her eyes. "Natalia." "I'm serious." "Then explain. I'll even stop decorating your diagram." "What exactly do you think the curse recognizes?" "Us." "No. Think." Lynleit exhaled through her nose. Natalia had used that tone in lectures too. "The people who killed it," she said. "And what makes you the same person now?" "I called you so you could answer questions, not sit me down for an examination." "Unfortunately, you've always needed both." "Only because you refuse to send the answers." "The ego," Natalia said. "Jung describes it as 'a complex of ideas which constitutes the centre of my field of consciousness.' Put that down. Leave space underneath." "For the translation?" "For your objections. The ego isn't the whole mind. It's the part around which you arrange what you consciously call yours. Your decisions, your memories, your intentions. You can forget what you ate yesterday without ceasing to recognize yourself." "I haven't forgotten. I object to calling it food." "Then the memory is doing very well." Lynleit wrote the definition. "So the curse doesn't need every memory intact." "That would be my first objection to erasing them. You might lose a year and still make the same choices for the same reasons. We need to know what it would take for its old description of you to stop being enough." "Can you measure that?" "I once thought I could. I kept a notebook of my decisions for three weeks. Every choice, followed by the reason I thought I'd made it." "How many notebooks?" "Too many. I was very pleased with them." "Always a warning." "Eventually I noticed that the woman in the notebooks was wonderfully reasonable. She never ate because she was bored. Never postponed a letter because she disliked the recipient. She had excellent reasons for everything." "You should introduce us." "I couldn't. I'd made her up. By the time I wrote down a choice, I'd already tidied it." Lynleit smiled and pushed the reports aside. "What did you try instead?" "I wrote down what I expected to do before I did it. Then what actually happened, including the little things I wanted to leave out. Tea, letters, unfinished work. The two columns disagreed much more often." "And that worked?" "It showed me where to look. It didn't explain every disagreement. Some days I was simply tired." Lynleit divided the space below the quotation into two columns. "Expectation and result." "Yes. For you, that means a new description of yourself is not enough. Calling yourself fearless doesn't remove a fear. Losing a title doesn't necessarily change how you make a decision. Changing clothes certainly won't help." "A pity. I could have been cured before lunch." "You're still looking for a procedure you can complete without anything happening to you." "I'm prepared to be mildly inconvenienced." "Lynleit." She put the pen down. "How much has to change?" "That I don't know." "Helpful." "I can give you a difference you already understand. When I left the Academy, I took my books home and thought I would begin all the work I'd been postponing." "And did you?" "I spent the first morning drafting a request to conduct it." Lynleit laughed once, then pressed a hand against her ribs. "To whom?" "An excellent question. I had nowhere to send it." "You could have sent it to me. I'd have approved it." "You would have corrected my handwriting." "Both. I'm generous." "I had stopped being a professor on paper. I was still waiting for someone to permit the next experiment. That habit took longer to notice. Longer still to stop." Lynleit picked up the pen again. "So handing in your resignation wasn't the whole change." "No. Nor would taking the title away from me now put me back where I was. I have done the work. Made mistakes I couldn't assign to the Academy. Paid for them myself." "And you still give examinations over the phone." "Some habits are worth keeping." Lynleit looked at the two names. "Trauma could do it." "It can. So can a religious conversion, grief, parenthood. But none is a reliable instruction. Two people can survive the same event and make very different things of it." "We already have a confrontation with death arranged." "Yes. I was hoping for something less terminal." "And both Kyrien and I would have to change." "Most likely. Go back to your sheet. You crossed out one name and could still recover it through the other." "So changing only me leaves him holding the old answer." "That is the risk. Whatever happens has to change what each of you is to the other." "Into what?" Natalia went quiet again. Lynleit knew that silence. It was the silence Natalia used immediately before saying something she knew would irritate her. "No." "I haven't said anything." "You were about to." "I was." "Natalia." "Fall in love." Lynleit stared at the phone. For several seconds neither spoke. Then Lynleit said, very carefully, "You cannot possibly be serious." "I am entirely serious." "You gave me homework, introduced me to Carl Jung, and told me about a dead substitute king so that you could tell me to fall in love?" "When you phrase it like that, it does sound theatrical." "I was trying to make it sound expensive. I don't intend to pay." "Think about an ordinary evening. You're absorbed in something. Someone you care about was meant to call an hour ago. You read the same sentence three times. You decide to work for another ten minutes before checking your phone." "And check it after two." "Thirty seconds, in my case. Myka was quite safe. I'd spent an hour pretending I could concentrate while I waited to hear it." "You could have called her." "I did. She asked whether I needed help with something." "Did you?" "I needed her to stop sounding so pleased with herself." Lynleit glanced at her own phone. "All right. Someone matters to you. How does that become enough to save us?" "It may not. Worrying over a missed call isn't a cure. But notice how much of an ordinary evening can already depend on someone else's safety. Now imagine finding you can't make plans for your own future without making room for that person. Even plans you never intend to show them." "That is sentimental nonsense." "No. Sentimental nonsense is what poets do with it afterward." Lynleit said nothing. "You don't have to become agreeable," Natalia added. "You may be thoroughly annoyed. The question is whether you still make the same decisions about your life once theirs has become part of it." "And whether they do the same." "Yes. That's why I'm talking about a reciprocal change. One person longing beautifully while the other carries on as before is no help to my hypothesis." "You make it sound like surgery." "At the moment, it is." "And how exactly do you prescribe falling in love with someone?" "You don't." "Then this is useless." "I didn't say it was convenient. You asked what might work." Lynleit closed her eyes. Natalia added, almost casually, "There are faster ways to produce similar changes, of course." Lynleit opened them again. "I dislike the way you said that." "You should." "What ways?" "Ask someone else." "Natalia." "I've already given you the academically respectable answer." "And the unrespectable one?" Natalia laughed softly. "Go speak to a priest." "You're enjoying this far too much." "I'm enjoying speaking to you. I'd prefer you weren't dying." Lynleit's hand tightened around the pen. "Then keep your afternoon free. I'm going to bring you a very unreasonable objection." "I look forward to it." After the call, Lynleit copied the two names onto a clean page. Underneath she wrote: What would have to change in both? She folded Natalia's first diagram and kept it inside the notebook. The unrespectable answer She sought a second opinion. Then a third. Eventually the investigation took her to Father Mikhail. His study smelled of wax, old wood, and something medicinal. Lynleit could not locate the last smell. Possibly it was the priest. Unlike Natalia, Mikhail had access to older Church records of curses attached to personal identity. He laid out several accounts while she took notes. Conversion had worked in some cases, marriage in others. War, parenthood, a confession followed by absolution: none had worked consistently. "So it isn't the marriage," Lynleit said. "Nor the certificate. The person afterward could no longer be described adequately as the person before." "And what would you recommend for Kyrien and me?" Mikhail folded his hands over his stomach. Nearly a minute passed. Lynleit straightened in her chair. Mikhail watched her with that particular priestly calm which sometimes preceded consolation, and sometimes something entirely unacceptable. "Do you understand your problem?" he asked. "I take it you have a theory." "I do." "Then I'm listening." He closed his eyes, rose, and went to the narrow window. In the evening light his cassock was almost black. When he spoke again, his voice had acquired the measured rise and fall of a chant. "O great warrior of the Divine Whore." Lynleit blinked. Her cup stopped halfway to her mouth. "O heir to the blood that stood at Inanna's gates, made covenants beneath her sign, and returned from her altars with what others had to take by the sword." She set the cup carefully on its saucer. "Father Mikhail, I'm not sure that wording is appropriate." "All the better. You're listening." He clasped his hands behind his back. "O daughter of a line that has carried its bond with the Cult through three thousand years. Through kingdoms, wars, prohibitions, reforms, and an inexhaustible supply of people convinced they had finally put an end to it." Lynleit lowered her eyes to the tea. She knew where this was going. There was still a possibility that he would stop out of common decency. Mikhail continued. "O heir to a tradition in which desire was power, intimacy could seal a bargain, the body could speak, and a bed could matter more to politics than a throne." "Father Mikhail." It was a very polite request. He looked at her, waited, and continued. "And here sits its representative." "Educated." He raised one finger. "Disciplined." A second. "Dangerous." A third. "Entirely familiar with her ancestry." Lynleit said nothing. "And yet..." He paused, apparently searching for the correct theological term. Lynleit closed her eyes. Mikhail noticed. "...catastrophically unsuited to the position." Her eyes opened. "I would ask you not to develop that thought." "Why?" "I doubt it will benefit either of us. Or your priesthood." "A reasonable objection." Her shoulders eased. "Overruled." Mikhail returned to the table, sat, adjusted his sleeve, and drank his tea. Then, in his ordinary voice: "Just have sex, loser." Lynleit stared at him. Mikhail drank his tea. She continued staring. He lowered the cup. "What?" She opened her mouth, then closed it. "You understood," he said. "I understood quite enough." "Excellent." "I didn't say I agreed." "I didn't ask whether you agreed." "You are a priest." "An observant one." "I think we're finished." "No. That was the introduction." She glanced at the door. "Retreat is hardly becoming of a warrior of Inanna, either." "You're beginning to abuse your knowledge of my family." "I'm using the pastoral material available." "My genealogy is not pastoral material." "Everything is pastoral material when the flock is sufficiently stubborn." Lynleit clasped her hands in her lap. "An association between two traditions does not automatically oblige anyone to reproduce every cultural feature of either." Mikhail raised an eyebrow. She stopped. "How interesting." "Don't." "I haven't said anything." "Which is why I'm asking you not to." He reached for his cup. "You've just supplied your own defence." "I stated a principle." "Of course." "A general principle." "Naturally." Lynleit looked at him. Mikhail remained perfectly composed. "Then you understand the charge." "I understand that you've decided to turn genealogy into harassment." She picked up her cup again, but did not drink. Mikhail watched. "Interesting." Her hand stopped. "What is?" "You can discuss murder, a coup, magical blackmail, and mass casualties in a perfectly even voice." She slowly returned the cup to its saucer. "One other human activity makes you an expert on porcelain." Lynleit looked at the saucer, then at him. "Perhaps the porcelain is behaving with more dignity than certain people present." He gave a quiet snort. "Good. Then let's leave theology out of it. You approach intimacy as an operation to be attempted after reconnaissance, risk assessment, political guarantees, and written opinions from several independent experts." "I came here about a curse." "And I am answering. If you like a man, you investigate him. If you like him a great deal, you begin counterintelligence." Her lips pressed together. "And when it becomes personal enough that neither is helping, you declare the matter irrelevant." Lynleit met his eyes, then looked away. For once, Mikhail did not comment. He drank his tea. "Thank you for the diagnosis." "An observation." "It has been noted." "In the voice of an official sending a document to an archive nobody will ever open." She glanced at the cup. This time she left it alone. "You seem to have confused my embarrassment with a treatment." "No. You asked whether something could change both of you enough for the curse to lose its hold. If an attachment already exists, physical intimacy might do that. What you trust him with, what you expect from him afterward, what he can no longer pretend you are to him. You would both have to change." "And if the attachment isn't sufficient?" "Then you will merely have had sex." Lynleit picked up her pen. "So you cannot promise anything." "No. I can tell you why this is a possibility. I cannot make it safe by explaining it until you stop blushing." "It is considerably easier for you to dispute three thousand years of religious continuity than admit to a thoroughly present-day problem." She wrote something, shut the notebook, and stood. "I think that is more than enough spiritual guidance for one visit." "You're leaving again." "I'm concluding the audience." "This is my study." Lynleit straightened her jacket. "All the more reason." She went to the door. "Lynleit." "What?" "You understand why this is so funny?" Her hand remained on the handle. Several seconds passed. "Unfortunately," she said, very quietly. "Then we have reached an understanding." She opened the door and looked back. Her face was composed again. "If you ever call me a warrior of the Divine Whore in front of anyone else, I will find a canonically permissible way to make your life considerably less pleasant." Mikhail considered this. "Better." "What?" "Some passion in that threat." She shut the door hard enough to rattle the cups. In the corridor, Lynleit opened her notebook. SEX? occupied most of the page. She nearly tore it out. In the study Mikhail waited until her footsteps had receded, then looked at the door. "Three thousand years of continuity." Another sip. "And the result." He sighed. "A virgin." A pause. "A disgrace to the institution." He went on drinking his tea. An alternative She did not tell Kyrien. He knew the prognosis, the failed attempts at suppression, and that she was still searching. He did not know what Natalia had told her. He did not know what Mikhail had told her. Most importantly, he did not know that Lynleit had begun treating their relationship as a possible procedure. At first she refused the idea. Then she investigated it. Then she attempted to disprove it. The Church called it transformation. Natalia called it reorganization of the ego. An old Magiarchal text called it discontinuity of identity; a thaumaturgical paper, failure of sympathetic recognition. Every source she consulted gave her another reason to return to the page she had nearly torn out. Meanwhile, their remaining weeks became days. Two days later Natalia called two days later. "So." "No." "I haven't asked anything." "You were about to." "I was." Lynleit continued reading. Finally Natalia said, "How do you feel about Kyrien now?" "The same." "Really." "Yes." "Nothing changed." "Nothing relevant." "Interesting distinction." "There is no distinction." "Of course." Lynleit turned a page she had not read. Natalia waited again. "The curse is gone," Lynleit said. "It is." "Kyrien is alive." "He is." "I am alive." "Also true." "The intervention therefore accomplished its purpose." Natalia made a thoughtful sound. "It failed." "It worked." "By failing." Lynleit closed the book. "There will not be another attempt." "I didn't suggest one." "There is no reason for one." "Correct." "The matter is resolved." "Completely." Lynleit narrowed her eyes. Natalia said nothing. That silence was intolerable. "There is absolutely no reason whatsoever for Kyrien and me to repeat anything that happened that evening." "I agree." "Good." "Good." Another silence. Then Natalia asked: "Are you disappointed?" Lynleit hung up. She opened the book again. The page was unfamiliar. So was the one before it. There had been a reason for that evening. A reason she could write down, defend, and blame on someone else. Now the curse was gone. She put the notebook under the book and tried to read. Kyrien's account Kyrien understood considerably less. He knew Lynleit had tried to sleep with him while behaving as though she were attempting an assassination. He knew she refused to explain why. He knew the curse had begun weakening the following morning. Any mention of that evening made her hostile enough to weaponize household items. There was a connection between these facts. He was missing something. This irritated him. Lynleit intended to keep it that way. The incomplete attempt and what followed had changed both of them enough for the curse to lose its hold. It could no longer recognize the exact pair of identities that had destroyed the Holumn. They survived. As far as Lynleit was concerned, the boundary between them remained uncrossed. Mostly. entries.text: Doom Has an Address · Version 1 · Alternate Chapter 07 · Later in Arc 1 After jointly destroying a Holumn, Lynleit and Kyrien inherit one fatal curse written across both identities and search for a way to survive without sacrificing either life. Lynleit and Kyrien destroy a Holumn together and complete the final condition of its mechanism. The Holumn transfers one terminal curse across both of their identities, causing progressive physical decline and a prognosis measured first in weeks and then in days. Suppressing the curse in either person fails because the remaining half reconstructs the other. The traditional solution requires one of them to die first so the surviving identity is released. Lynleit rejects that answer and searches Magiarchal, medical, theurgical, academic, and Church records for another form of identity discontinuity. Natalia identifies the attachment as sympathetic recognition of the ego and proposes profound reciprocal transformation as a possible alternative to death. Father Mikhail reaches the same conclusion through Church records and tells Lynleit that physical intimacy could work only if an existing attachment changes both identities. Lynleit withholds Natalia and Mikhail's proposed treatment from Kyrien. Lynleit initiates an awkward sexual encounter and Kyrien responds. Their reciprocal change makes the curse unable to recognize the exact pair of identities that destroyed the Holumn, causing the entanglement to fracture. Lynleit hiding the notebook page suggests that she still cannot discuss the attempt openly with Kyrien. inferred Doom Has an Address After the killing For several nights after they destroyed the Holumn, Lynleit blamed her exhaustion on the fight. Then small cuts stopped closing. Sleep left her as tired as she had been before it. Kyrien began pausing on stairs. He waited for her at the landings, which might have been considerate if she had not seen him trying to recover his breath. The examinations gave them weeks. Suppressing the curse in Lynleit brought brief relief. It returned through Kyrien. Treating him produced the same result in reverse. Whatever had followed them out of the fight was attached to both of them. One could survive if the other died first. "No," Lynleit said. She took the reports away and began calling people who had not yet given her that answer. The Magiarchal records led her to physicians, prohibited theurgical procedures, and arguments about what counted as a person. Memory erasure would not work. Neither would a coma. Destroying magical capacity offered no reliable prospect, and having someone declared dead would change nothing. Eventually she called Natalia. The former professor Natalia was silent long enough that Lynleit checked the connection. "I'm reading," she said. "You sent six reports." "The last two are the same treatment. On different patients." "I noticed." Lynleit leaned against the desk. Her hand had begun trembling again. She put the telephone in the other one. "The Holumn transferred its death to whoever killed it," Natalia said. "You killed it together. That's why treating either of you separately fails." "They've established that." "They've established what happens. I'm asking what it recognizes." Lynleit looked at the reports. "Us." "Your bodies? Your names? The people you understand yourselves to be?" She had used that tone in lectures. Lynleit had once liked being the student who could answer her. "The ego," she said. "Good. Now tell me why it has to be destroyed." "Because it keeps reconstructing the curse." "And death is the only thing that can change a person?" Lynleit stopped looking at the reports. Natalia spoke about substitute kings, human-shaped vessels used in purification rites, and stories in which a life was hidden outside its body. Lynleit let her finish the first example, interrupted the second, and had to ask her to repeat the third. "These aren't your curse," Natalia said. "But the point of attachment isn't always where you'd expect. Something can recognize a role or a relationship. In this case it recognizes the two people responsible for one act." "Could we make it recognize someone else?" "You need to stop being the people it recognizes." "Memory erasure doesn't work." "Because your memories aren't all of you. Nor is your title, or your name, or the description you'd give a stranger. Jung's ego isn't the whole psyche either, but it is a useful place to begin: the conscious sense of who you are. That can change without killing you." "How much would we have to change?" "That I don't know." Lynleit rubbed her forehead. "Conversion," Natalia continued. "Grief. Parenthood, sometimes. An experience that makes your old assumptions impossible to live by. The trouble is getting there deliberately, and getting both of you there before the curse restores what you've changed." "We're already confronting death." "I was hoping for something you could survive." "Then suggest it." Natalia went quiet. "No," Lynleit said. "I haven't said anything." "You were about to." "I was." "Natalia." "Fall in love." Lynleit took the telephone away from her ear and looked at it. "You cannot possibly be serious." "I am." "You've taken me through death rituals and Carl Jung to tell me to fall in love?" "You asked for an alternative." "I asked for something we can do." "And I can't prescribe it. You can't pretend your way out of this. But if you already matter enough to each other, there may be something to work with." Lynleit looked toward the door. "How would we know?" "You'd have to risk finding out." There were faster possibilities, Natalia admitted. She declined to describe them. "Go speak to a priest." A second opinion Father Mikhail had records Natalia could not consult. He laid them out while Lynleit took notes. Conversion had broken one attachment. Marriage had broken another. Other accounts concerned war, parenthood, and a confession followed by absolution that had only partly succeeded. Lynleit put a mark beside the partial result. "So confession isn't enough." "In that case, no." "And marriage?" "Neither is a certificate." She looked up. "These people changed," he said. "The records tell us when. They don't give us a rite that will make it happen to you." The list occupied most of a page. She had already crossed out more than half of it. "What would you recommend for Kyrien and me?" Mikhail looked at her notebook, then at her. "Just have sex, loser." Lynleit became red from her throat to her ears. "What?" "You heard me." "You are a priest." "An observant one." She stood and took her coat. "Lynleit. There are theological reasons." She reached the door. "Sex is not the important part." Her hand remained on the handle. "If the attachment is already there, acting on it may change what you are to each other. Enough to break the recognition. I cannot promise you that it will." "And if it doesn't?" "Then you will merely have had sex." She left before he could add anything. In the corridor she discovered that she had written SEX? across the middle of her notebook. She nearly tore the page out. Days Kyrien knew the prognosis and the failed treatments. When he asked about her research, she told him she was still checking something. She checked it against a Magiarchal text, then a thaumaturgical paper. Neither gave her a dependable way to measure the change. Both gave her reasons to keep thinking about it. She tried to imagine explaining the proposed treatment to Kyrien. She got as far as his expression and shut the notebook. By then he tired after ordinary errands. She had to steady her wrist to write. Their remaining time was measured in days. The evening Kyrien noticed the second change of clothes. "Are we going somewhere?" "No." "Then why..." "Is there something wrong with this?" He stopped asking. Later she corrected him over something that needed no correction and spent several minutes avoiding his eyes. "Is this about the curse?" A cushion hit him in the face. He lowered it. "Lynleit." "Don't." "I asked a question." "Ask another one." She had expected to recognize the right moment. Instead they sat beside each other on the sofa, tired and frightened, discussing something she could not keep her mind on. Kyrien said her name. She looked at him. Then she moved closer before she could find another reason to wait. He was surprised. She gave him time to understand, and he answered her. The encounter that followed was sudden and awkward, with little of the composure she had imagined bringing to it. The curse became unstable while they were together. For several seconds they felt it searching for something in them, returning to the same place and failing to settle. Its hold fractured. Neither had cast a spell. Their attachment had changed both identities enough to disrupt the curse's recognition. The encounter had brought that change about; it had no curative power of its own. They survived. Lynleit still had the page in her notebook. She folded it under the next one before Kyrien could see. Lynleit,Kyrien,Natalia,Father Mikhail

entries.text: Doom Has an Address · Version 2 · Superseded Chapter 07 · Later in Arc 1 After Lynleit and Kyrien inherit one fatal curse across both identities, an incomplete attempt at intimacy is followed by the curse's collapse and leaves the exact threshold of their transformation unresolved. Lynleit and Kyrien destroy a Holumn together and complete the final condition of its mechanism. The Holumn transfers one terminal curse across both identities, causing progressive physical decline and a prognosis measured first in weeks and then in days. Suppressing the curse in either person fails because the remaining attachment reconstructs it in the other. The traditional solution requires one of them to die first so the surviving identity is released. Lynleit rejects that answer and searches Magiarchal, medical, theurgical, academic, and Church records for another form of identity discontinuity. Natalia identifies the attachment as sympathetic recognition of the ego and proposes profound reciprocal transformation as a possible alternative to death. Father Mikhail reaches the same conclusion through Church records and tells Lynleit that physical intimacy could work only if an existing attachment changes both identities. Lynleit withholds the proposed method from Kyrien and investigates their relationship as a possible procedure. Lynleit attempts to initiate an encounter but does not fully cross the boundary between them. The curse begins weakening the following morning and is later gone. Her prepared answer suggests that Lynleit expected, and had been thinking about, another conversation with Kyrien. inferred Doom Has an Address After the killing For several nights after they destroyed the Holumn, Lynleit blamed her exhaustion on the fight. Then small cuts stopped closing. Sleep left her as tired as she had been before it. Kyrien began pausing on stairs. He waited for her at the landings, which might have been considerate if she had not seen him trying to recover his breath. The examinations gave them weeks. Suppressing the curse in Lynleit brought brief relief. It returned through Kyrien. Treating him produced the same result in reverse. Whatever had followed them out of the fight was attached to both of them. One could survive if the other died first. "No," Lynleit said. She took the reports away and began calling people who had not yet given her that answer. The Magiarchal records led her to physicians, prohibited theurgical procedures, and arguments about what counted as a person. Memory erasure would not work. Neither would a coma. Destroying magical capacity offered no reliable prospect, and having someone declared dead would change nothing. Eventually she called Natalia. The former professor Natalia was silent long enough that Lynleit checked the connection. "I'm reading," she said. "You sent six reports." "The last two are the same treatment. On different patients." "I noticed." Lynleit leaned against the desk. Her hand had begun trembling again. She put the telephone in the other one. "The Holumn transferred its death to whoever killed it," Natalia said. "You killed it together. That's why treating either of you separately fails." "They've established that." "They've established what happens. I'm asking what it recognizes." Lynleit looked at the reports. "Us." "Your bodies? Your names? The people you understand yourselves to be?" She had used that tone in lectures. Lynleit had once liked being the student who could answer her. "The ego," she said. "Good. Now tell me why it has to be destroyed." "Because it keeps reconstructing the curse." "And death is the only thing that can change a person?" Lynleit stopped looking at the reports. Natalia spoke about substitute kings, human-shaped vessels used in purification rites, and stories in which a life was hidden outside its body. Lynleit let her finish the first example, interrupted the second, and had to ask her to repeat the third. "These aren't your curse," Natalia said. "But the point of attachment isn't always where you'd expect. Something can recognize a role or a relationship. In this case it recognizes the two people responsible for one act." "Could we make it recognize someone else?" "You need to stop being the people it recognizes." "Memory erasure doesn't work." "Because your memories aren't all of you. Nor is your title, or your name, or the description you'd give a stranger. Jung's ego isn't the whole psyche either, but it is a useful place to begin: the conscious sense of who you are. That can change without killing you." "How much would we have to change?" "That I don't know." Lynleit rubbed her forehead. "Conversion," Natalia continued. "Grief. Parenthood, sometimes. An experience that makes your old assumptions impossible to live by. The trouble is getting there deliberately, and getting both of you there before the curse restores what you've changed." "We're already confronting death." "I was hoping for something you could survive." "Then suggest it." Natalia went quiet. "No," Lynleit said. "I haven't said anything." "You were about to." "I was." "Natalia." "Fall in love." Lynleit took the telephone away from her ear and looked at it. "You cannot possibly be serious." "I am." "You've taken me through death rituals and Carl Jung to tell me to fall in love?" "You asked for an alternative." "I asked for something we can do." "And I can't prescribe it. You can't pretend your way out of this. But if you already matter enough to each other, there may be something to work with." Lynleit looked toward the door. "How would we know?" "You'd have to risk finding out." There were faster possibilities, Natalia admitted. She declined to describe them. "Go speak to a priest." A second opinion Father Mikhail had records Natalia could not consult. He laid them out while Lynleit took notes. Conversion had broken one attachment. Marriage had broken another. Other accounts concerned war, parenthood, and a confession followed by absolution that had only partly succeeded. Lynleit put a mark beside the partial result. "So confession isn't enough." "In that case, no." "And marriage?" "Neither is a certificate." She looked up. "These people changed," he said. "The records tell us when. They don't give us a rite that will make it happen to you." The list occupied most of a page. She had already crossed out more than half of it. "What would you recommend for Kyrien and me?" Mikhail looked at her notebook, then at her. "Just have sex, loser." Lynleit became red from her throat to her ears. "What?" "You heard me." "You are a priest." "An observant one." She stood and took her coat. "Lynleit. There are theological reasons." She reached the door. "Sex is not the important part." Her hand remained on the handle. "If the attachment is already there, acting on it may change what you are to each other. Enough to break the recognition. I cannot promise you that it will." "And if it doesn't?" "Then you will merely have had sex." She left before he could add anything. In the corridor she discovered that she had written SEX? across the middle of her notebook. She nearly tore the page out. Days Kyrien knew the prognosis and the failed treatments. When he asked about her research, she told him she was still checking something. She checked it against a Magiarchal text, then a thaumaturgical paper. Neither gave her a dependable way to measure the change. Both gave her reasons to keep thinking about it. She tried to imagine explaining the proposed treatment to Kyrien. She got as far as his expression and shut the notebook. By then he tired after ordinary errands. She had to steady her wrist to write. Their remaining time was measured in days. Two days later Natalia called while Lynleit was reading. "So." "No." "I haven't asked anything." "You were about to." "I was." Lynleit kept her eyes on the page. "How do you feel about Kyrien now?" "The same." "Nothing changed?" "Nothing relevant." "Interesting distinction." "There is no distinction." Lynleit turned a page she had not read. "The curse is gone," she said. "Yes." "We're alive. The intervention accomplished its purpose." "I thought you said the attempt failed." "It did." "Then it wasn't necessary to finish." Lynleit closed the book. "There will not be another attempt." "I didn't suggest one." "There is no reason for one." "Correct." "The matter is resolved." Natalia let her wait. "There is absolutely no reason for Kyrien and me to repeat anything that happened that evening." "I agree." "Good." Another silence. Then Natalia asked, "Are you disappointed?" Lynleit hung up. The book was open again before she remembered that she had lost her place. She went back a page. That one was unfamiliar too. The missing explanation Kyrien knew she had tried to sleep with him. He had not known she could approach it with quite so much anger. The curse had begun weakening the following morning. Now it was gone. When he asked her about that evening, she refused to explain. When he mentioned the improvement, she said she was glad. He was glad too. He still wanted to know what had happened. She had not told him what Natalia and Mikhail proposed, and he could not connect the attempt to their recovery without it. Asking again seemed likely to bring another household object at his head. Whatever Lynleit had planned, they had not completed it. The attempt and what followed had nevertheless changed them enough for the curse to lose its hold. He left the subject alone when they next met. She had prepared an answer. There was no occasion to use it. Lynleit,Kyrien,Natalia,Father Mikhail

entries.text: Doom Has an Address · Version 3 · Superseded Chapter 07 · Later in Arc 1 A shared curse sends Lynleit from Natalia's scholarship to Father Mikhail's blunt advice. After an incomplete attempt at intimacy, she has recovered but still has questions she refuses to discuss. Lynleit and Kyrien destroy a Holumn together and complete the final condition of its mechanism. The Holumn transfers one terminal curse across both identities, causing progressive physical decline and a prognosis measured first in weeks and then in days. Suppressing the curse in either person fails because the remaining attachment reconstructs it in the other. The traditional solution requires one of them to die first so the surviving identity is released. Lynleit rejects the fatal solution, consults other Magi, and searches Magiarchal records and prohibited theurgical procedures for an alternative. Natalia proposes that the curse recognizes the ego, quotes Jung's definition, and suggests reciprocal transformation as an alternative to death. Father Mikhail reaches the same conclusion through Church records and tells Lynleit that physical intimacy could work only if an existing attachment changes both identities. Lynleit withholds the proposed method from Kyrien and investigates their relationship as a possible procedure. Lynleit attempts to initiate an encounter but does not fully cross the boundary between them. The curse begins weakening the following morning and is later gone. Lynleit's unread pages and repeated denials suggest that she still wants Kyrien now that the curse is gone. inferred Kyrien knows about Lynleit's attempt, her refusal to explain it, and the curse's decline, but lacks enough information to connect them. The incomplete attempt and its aftermath change both identities enough for the curse to lose its hold. Doom Has an Address The condition The Holumn was eventually destroyed. That was the first mistake. Lynleit and Kyrien did not understand what they were fighting until after they had already killed it. Destroying the creature completed the final part of its mechanism: its own terminal condition passed to whoever had caused its death. They had destroyed it together. There was still only one curse, attached to both of them. Their bodies began to weaken. Sleep stopped restoring them properly, and minor injuries healed too slowly. Lynleit found her magecraft increasingly exhausting. Kyrien began stopping on stairs. Within days, ordinary exertion had become difficult for both of them. The Magi who examined the curse gave them several weeks. Attempts to suppress it produced a second discovery. Removing it from Lynleit brought relief only until the attachment to Kyrien restored it. Treating him produced the same result in reverse. One of them could survive if the other died first. Lynleit rejected the answer. She spoke to other Magi, searched Magiarchal records, and investigated prohibited theurgical procedures. Could memory erasure work? A coma? Destroying magical capacity? Every answer sent her back to the same choice. Having one of them declared dead would not help either. The curse had no interest in legal language. Eventually she called Natalia. The academically respectable answer Natalia was silent long enough that Lynleit checked the connection. "This is older than your Holumn," she said at last. "Not the creature itself. The mechanism. People have been inventing versions of it for thousands of years." Lynleit leaned back against the desk. "Such as?" "The Assyrians had a substitute-king ritual. If an omen predicted the king's death, they could install another man in his place and let the omen fall on him instead. The important part wasn't biology. It was identity. For the duration of the rite, that man occupied the position the omen recognized as king." "Comforting." "It gets worse. Japanese purification rites used human-shaped substitutes to receive pollution or misfortune from a person. Folklore is full of beings whose life is hidden somewhere outside their bodies. An egg, an animal, a box, a tree. Destroying the body does nothing because the actual point of attachment is elsewhere." Lynleit frowned. "You're saying the Holumn did the same thing." "Almost. It inverted the principle." Natalia's voice became more focused. "It hid its death in the people who killed it." Lynleit said nothing. "And then there is the old logic of sympathetic magic," Natalia continued. "Things that have been joined remain connected after separation. Hair, blood, possessions, names, vows. Primitive language for a phenomenon your Magi would dress up with considerably more mathematics." "So when Kyrien and I destroyed it together..." "You didn't each receive half a curse. That would be easier. You became two coordinates of the same one." Lynleit looked down at her hand. "If I suppress mine, his restores it." "Because the structure still resolves correctly. Kyrien exists. You exist. Both of you remain sufficiently identical to the people who performed the act. The curse checks its address and finds both occupants still at home." "Then the usual solution really is what they told me." "One dies first." The words settled badly between them. Lynleit stared out the window. "I'm not doing that." "I assumed as much." "There has to be another way." "There usually is. People just become lazy when death works reliably." Lynleit closed her eyes. "Natalia." "I'm serious." "Then explain." Another pause. "What exactly do you think the curse recognizes?" "Us." "No. Think." Lynleit exhaled through her nose. Natalia had used that tone in lectures too. "The people who killed it," she said. "And what makes you the same person now?" "I called you so you could answer questions, not sit me down for an examination." "Unfortunately, you've always needed both." "Natalia." "The ego," Natalia said. "That's where I would begin. Jung describes it as 'a complex of ideas which constitutes the centre of my field of consciousness.' Not the whole psyche. The conscious sense of identity. The part that says this is me, this happened to me, this is what I want, this is where I end and the rest of the world begins." Lynleit straightened slightly. Natalia continued. "If the curse attached itself to that structure, then biological death is merely the most absolute way of disrupting it. It isn't necessarily the only way." Lynleit was quiet now. "You think the ego can change enough that the curse stops recognizing it." "Exactly." "How much?" "That I don't know." "Helpful." "I can tell you what would not be enough. New clothes. A new title. Hypnosis. Memory tampering at the surface level. Pretending to become someone else. The change would have to reach the architecture beneath ordinary self-description." "What kind of change?" "The kind after which a person can truthfully say that the one who entered an event and the one who emerged from it are not psychologically identical." Lynleit looked toward the floor. "Trauma," Natalia said. "Religious conversion. Surviving something that forces a complete reorganization of one's values. Grief can do it. Parenthood sometimes does it. A genuine confrontation with death certainly can." "We already have one of those arranged." "Yes. I was hoping for something less terminal." Lynleit rubbed her forehead. "And you think both Kyrien and I would have to change?" "Most likely. The curse is relational. Altering one coordinate might destabilize it, but if the other remains intact it may simply reconstruct the original pattern. You need to damage the relation itself." "Damage?" "Change, if you prefer a nicer word." "Into what?" Natalia went quiet again. Lynleit knew that silence. It was the silence Natalia used immediately before saying something she knew would irritate her. "No." "I haven't said anything." "You were about to." "I was." "Natalia." "Fall in love." Lynleit stared at the phone. For several seconds neither spoke. Then Lynleit said, very carefully, "You cannot possibly be serious." "I am entirely serious." "You spent the last ten minutes explaining Assyrian death rituals, sympathetic magic, external souls and Carl Jung so that you could tell me to fall in love?" "When you phrase it like that, it does sound theatrical." "Natalia." "Love is one of the few ordinary human experiences capable of reorganizing identity at several levels simultaneously. Future, loyalty, fear, attachment, self-image, boundaries. People begin making decisions as though another person has partially entered the structure of the self." "That is sentimental nonsense." "No. Sentimental nonsense is what poets do with it afterward." Lynleit said nothing. "If the Holumn's curse is anchored to where each of you draws the boundary between self and other," Natalia continued, "then a sufficiently profound reciprocal attachment could distort that boundary enough to break the original configuration." "You make it sound like surgery." "At the moment, it is." "And how exactly do you prescribe falling in love with someone?" "You don't." "Then this is useless." "I didn't say it was convenient. You asked what might work." Lynleit closed her eyes. Natalia added, almost casually, "There are faster ways to produce similar changes, of course." Lynleit opened them again. "I dislike the way you said that." "You should." "What ways?" "Ask someone else." "Natalia." "I've already given you the academically respectable answer." "And the unrespectable one?" Natalia laughed softly. "Go speak to a priest." Lynleit eventually hung up with considerably more knowledge and considerably less dignity than she had possessed before making the call. The unrespectable answer She sought a second opinion. Then a third. Eventually the investigation took her to Father Mikhail. Unlike Natalia, Mikhail had access to older theological records concerning curses that attach themselves to personal identity rather than flesh or soul. His conclusion was disturbingly similar. The Church had encountered analogous phenomena before. Not identical curses, but conditions in which an entity remained attached to a person's psychic continuity. Conversion sometimes worked. Marriage occasionally worked. Surviving war sometimes worked. Parenthood had worked once. A profound confession followed by absolution had produced partial success in another case. None of these things were magical rituals in themselves. The common element was transformation. An old organization of the self ceased to be sufficient. Something new replaced it. Mikhail explained this patiently while Lynleit took notes. Then she reached the practical question. "What would you recommend for Kyrien and me?" Mikhail looked at her. Lynleit waited. The priest appeared to consider several centuries of theology. Then he said, completely straight-faced: "Just have sex, loser." Silence. Lynleit became red from her throat to her ears. "What?" "You heard me." "You are a priest." "An observant one." She stood. "Lynleit." She grabbed her coat. "There are theological reasons." She headed for the door. "Lynleit." She opened it. "Sex is not the important part." She stopped. Mikhail remained seated. "The important part is what happens when two people who have spent years maintaining separate identities voluntarily cross a boundary that neither can afterward pretend was never crossed." Lynleit slowly turned around. "If there is already sufficient attachment between you, physical intimacy may produce exactly the discontinuity you need. Body, trust, vulnerability, future expectation, shame, desire, identity. Several layers of the psyche move at once." "And if there isn't sufficient attachment?" "Then you will merely have had sex." Her expression became murderous. Mikhail shrugged. "Which is why I recommend choosing your partner carefully." She left. Only in the corridor did Lynleit realize that she had written SEX? in enormous letters across the middle of her notebook. She nearly tore the page out. An alternative She did not tell Kyrien. He knew the prognosis, the failed attempts at suppression, and that she was still searching. He did not know what Natalia had told her. He did not know what Mikhail had told her. Most importantly, he did not know that Lynleit had begun treating their relationship as a possible procedure. At first she refused the idea. Then she investigated it. Then she attempted to disprove it. The Church called it transformation. Natalia called it reorganization of the ego. An old Magiarchal text called it discontinuity of identity; a thaumaturgical paper, failure of sympathetic recognition. Every source she consulted gave her another reason to return to the page she had nearly torn out. Meanwhile, their remaining weeks became days. Two days later Natalia called two days later. "So." "No." "I haven't asked anything." "You were about to." "I was." Lynleit continued reading. Finally Natalia said, "How do you feel about Kyrien now?" "The same." "Really." "Yes." "Nothing changed." "Nothing relevant." "Interesting distinction." "There is no distinction." "Of course." Lynleit turned a page she had not read. Natalia waited again. "The curse is gone," Lynleit said. "It is." "Kyrien is alive." "He is." "I am alive." "Also true." "The intervention therefore accomplished its purpose." Natalia made a thoughtful sound. "It failed." "It worked." "By failing." Lynleit closed the book. "There will not be another attempt." "I didn't suggest one." "There is no reason for one." "Correct." "The matter is resolved." "Completely." Lynleit narrowed her eyes. Natalia said nothing. That silence was intolerable. "There is absolutely no reason whatsoever for Kyrien and me to repeat anything that happened that evening." "I agree." "Good." "Good." Another silence. Then Natalia asked: "Are you disappointed?" Lynleit hung up. She opened the book again. The page was unfamiliar. So was the one before it. There had been a reason for that evening. A reason she could write down, defend, and blame on someone else. Now the curse was gone. She put the notebook under the book and tried to read. Kyrien's account Kyrien understood considerably less. He knew Lynleit had tried to sleep with him while behaving as though she were attempting an assassination. He knew she refused to explain why. He knew the curse had begun weakening the following morning. Any mention of that evening made her hostile enough to weaponize household items. There was a connection between these facts. He was missing something. This irritated him. Lynleit intended to keep it that way. The incomplete attempt and what followed had changed both of them enough for the curse to lose its hold. It could no longer recognize the exact pair of identities that had destroyed the Holumn. They survived. As far as Lynleit was concerned, the boundary between them remained uncrossed. Mostly. Lynleit,Kyrien,Natalia,Father Mikhail

entries.title: The Bench under the Lamp · v1
entries.subtitle: Chapter 08 · Later in Arc 1
entries.text: The Bench under the Lamp · v1 Chapter 08 · Later in Arc 1 An evening walk leaves Lynleit and Kyrien beneath a park lamp. A joke about their failed attempt becomes a private encounter, followed by an unexpected request for his flask. Lynleit and Kyrien walk through the quarantined park after work, lose their way, and stop at a bench beneath a lamppost. Kyrien takes one small drink from his flask after the long day and returns it to its usual pocket. Their comfortable proximity and teasing bring up the failed curse encounter months earlier. Lynleit has spent the intervening months researching intimacy; the opportunity on the bench is spontaneous. They kiss, and the scene cuts away before the private encounter. The cut away and Lynleit's later claim of successful research indicate that their intimacy has progressed beyond the failed attempt. inferred Lynleit calls the research successful, and they leave the bench before Kyrien asks whether she intends to win arguments this way. Her delayed request for whiskey and refusal to explain suggest an unexpected practical consequence without undoing her satisfaction. inferred Kyrien hands her the flask without pressing for an explanation, and they continue walking. The Bench under the Lamp The path divided again. Lynleit stopped at the fork and looked back. Kyrien was looking back too. "That is unhelpful," she said. "I didn't put it there." They had finished work before the light began to fail. The park still lay between them and a sensible end to the evening. Neither had been particularly diligent about finding the shortest way through it. Kyrien took out his flask. One small drink, then the cap went back on. Lynleit waited while he returned it to the same pocket. "Medicine?" "Long day." She chose the left path. He followed without offering a better one. After a while, a lamppost appeared between the trees. Beneath it stood a bench with a dry seat. Kyrien sat down. "We've established one thing," Lynleit said. "That you chose left?" "That this path has a bench." He moved his elbow. She sat beside him, closer than the available space required, and leaned back. Beyond the light, the path continued into trees they had already spent too much of the day looking at. Her shoulder rested against his. Neither moved it. "You could admit you don't know the way," he said. "I know several ways. I'm choosing between them." "You've tried that answer before." She turned her head. "When?" He looked at her for a moment. "The evening you wouldn't explain anything." "You'll have to be considerably more specific." "The curse." Lynleit studied a loose thread at her cuff. The curse had been gone for months. His memory, unfortunately, had made a complete recovery too. "We survived." "I noticed." "Then your complaint seems poorly founded." "It was a question." She let her hand fall between them. He glanced at it, then back at her face. There had been quite a lot of reading since that evening. Some of it had been useful. Some had disagreed so confidently with the rest that she had wanted to mark it and send it back. None of it had suggested a park bench. "What?" Kyrien asked. "Nothing." "You're looking at me." "You are very near." "You sat there." She smiled at that, reluctantly. Then she kissed him. For a moment, he remained as still as he did before committing to a bad hand of cards. She drew back enough to look at him. "You can stop calculating," she said. "I was going to say that to you." This time, when she leaned toward him, he met her halfway. Afterward They remained beneath the lamp a little longer. Lynleit straightened her cuff. Kyrien watched her with an expression she would have liked to preserve for later reference. "Research was a success," she said. "Thanks for your participation." He looked down at the bench, then at her. "Research." "You're welcome." She stood and checked that she had everything. He took a little longer to get up. "We should probably determine where we are." "Now?" "You were the one who stopped walking." They left the lamp behind. For several minutes Lynleit was excellent company. She did not object when he chose a turning. She even allowed him to finish a sentence about their route. "Is this how you're going to win arguments from now on?" "You wish. Not a chance." He made no attempt to contest the result. They walked farther. Lynleit swallowed, frowned briefly, and continued. A few steps later the frown returned. She stopped. "Give me your whiskey." "Why?" "You don't need to know." His hand went to the familiar pocket. He passed her the flask without another question. She drank, screwed the cap back on, and returned it. "This way," she said. Kyrien followed. Lynleit,Kyrien

Kyrien takes one small drink from his flask after the long day and returns it to its usual pocket. Their comfortable proximity and teasing bring up the failed curse encounter months earlier. Lynleit has spent the intervening months researching intimacy; the opportunity on the bench is spontaneous. Lynleit rests her head in Kyrien’s lap. Lynleit’s satisfaction and claim of successful research indicate progress beyond the earlier failed encounter. inferred Lynleit calls the research successful, and they leave the bench before Kyrien asks whether she intends to win arguments this way. Her delayed request for whiskey and refusal to explain suggest an unexpected practical consequence without undoing her satisfaction. inferred Kyrien hands her the flask without pressing for an explanation, and they continue walking. The Bench under the Lamp The path divided again. Lynleit stopped at the fork and looked back. Kyrien was looking back too. "That is unhelpful," she said. "I didn't put it there." They had finished work before the light began to fail. The park still lay between them and a sensible end to the evening. Neither had been particularly diligent about finding the shortest way through it. Kyrien took out his flask. One small drink, then the cap went back on. Lynleit waited while he returned it to the same pocket. "Medicine?" "Long day." She chose the left path. He followed without offering a better one. After a while, a lamppost appeared between the trees. Beneath it stood a bench with a dry seat. Kyrien sat down. "We've established one thing," Lynleit said. "That you chose left?" "That this path has a bench." He moved his elbow. She sat beside him, closer than the available space required, and leaned back. Beyond the light, the path continued into trees they had already spent too much of the day looking at. Her shoulder rested against his. Neither moved it. "You could admit you don't know the way," he said. "I know several ways. I'm choosing between them." "You've tried that answer before." She turned her head. "When?" He looked at her for a moment. "The evening you wouldn't explain anything." "You'll have to be considerably more specific." "The curse." Lynleit studied a loose thread at her cuff. The curse had been gone for months. His memory, unfortunately, had made a complete recovery too. "We survived." "I noticed." "Then your complaint seems poorly founded." "It was a question." She let her hand fall between them. He glanced at it, then back at her face. There had been quite a lot of reading since that evening. Some of it had been useful. Some had disagreed so confidently with the rest that she had wanted to mark it and send it back. None of it had suggested a park bench. "What?" Kyrien asked. "Nothing." "You're looking at me." "You are very near." "You sat there." She shifted along the bench and rested her head in his lap. Above her, Kyrien looked down without finding anything to say. For once, she let him take his time. [WRITER: The private encounter belongs here. Complete the omitted passage from the archived scene source; no replacement kiss is intended. The aftermath below resumes after this gap.] Afterward They remained beneath the lamp a little longer. Lynleit straightened her cuff. Kyrien watched her with an expression she would have liked to preserve for later reference. "Research was successful," she said. "Thank you for your participation." He looked down at the bench, then at her. "Research." "You're welcome." She stood and checked that she had everything. He took a little longer to get up. "We should probably determine where we are." "Now?" "You were the one who stopped walking." They left the lamp behind. For several minutes Lynleit was excellent company. She did not object when he chose a turning. She even allowed him to finish a sentence about their route. "Is this how you're going to win arguments from now on?" "You wish. Not a chance." He made no attempt to contest the result. They walked farther. Lynleit swallowed, frowned briefly, and continued. A few steps later the frown returned. She stopped. "Give me your whiskey." "Why?" "You don't need to know." His hand went to the familiar pocket. He passed her the flask without another question. She drank, screwed the cap back on, and returned it. "This way," she said. Kyrien followed. Lynleit,Kyrien
